utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. May I introduce Alexandra Doyle, who has been with the team since the beginning of January but leaves us now for the European Commission. She is a graduate of Oxford University and has a LL.M. from Edinburgh University. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, yesterday in answer to a question from Dr. Karadzic about the Varian A and B instructions, you emphasised: "It meant nothing to me and I did not even take it at the Holiday Inn conference room when it was distributed." That's at transcript page 32013. The reason you didn't take a copy of the Variant A and B instructions is because Mr. Vjestica, the SDS president of Bosanska Krupa, was also present at the Holiday Inn and as the document was marked strictly confidential, between the two of you, you took only one copy and it was Mr. Vjestica who took the copy back to Bosanska Krupa acquaint the local SDS membership with its contents; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I think it was as you described it. Because he was the president of the Municipal Board of the SDS and I was the deputy. I was in the know, but Mr. Vjestica was present when those texts were distributed. He was a delegate in the club. Both the Main Board and the club often had joint sessions because the composition of both -- both bodies was the same.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I could have 65 ter 26007, page 32 of the English and page 29 of the B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, this is the portion of your interview with the OTP where you speak about this. And at line 9 in the English and at line 11 in the B/C/S, you're shown a document with a reference number that is, in fact, the Variant A and B instructions. Those are the reference numbers for P5 in evidence in this case. And at line 12 you're asked in -- in the English, and at line 14 in the B/C/S, you're asked: "When was the first you knew of these instructions?" And you explain about the session of the Main Board and that the document was adopted. And then you're asked: "So you were there when it was presented to you?" And you answer: "Yes." And then you were asked if you took a copy back to Bosanska Krupa and you say: "I think the deputy took it on because it had strictly confidential marks so we didn't necessarily take more than one copy, and he was the local party president anyway so he just took it to acquaint the SDS membership with it." And you're asked if that is Mr. Vjestica you're talking about and you say: "Yes." Does that remind you that at this meeting at the Holiday Inn, it was Mr. Vjestica who took the copy of the Variant A and B instructions back to Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe yes; but maybe no. It was a long time ago, you see, and that document, since I was up to date -- I had all the up-to-date information, I don't remember that document so precisely because it didn't -- it wasn't binding on me to do anything because there were the existing laws of Yugoslavia and the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that were in force. And why deal with these instructions. This was, by the way, the answer I had to give, because the investigators wouldn't talk about anything else but the instructions. Whenever I mentioned a law, they would say, No, that's not a problem, we're only interested in the instructions, as if the instructions had been God given.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Klickovic, immediately after this exchange, you concede that you -- of your own accord volunteer the information and pursuant to these instructions, instructions on the party activities in Krupa were compiled. And investigator says: "I think we have a copy of those. We'll get to them in a minute." And then he says: "So pursuant to the document that we were talking about, Bosanska Krupa also adopted the instruction for the work of the SDS party within the municipality of Bosanska Krupa; right?" And you say: "Yes." And then the investigator shows you a document and asks you if it's your signature on the last page, and you say: "I think so." And then you're asked -- sorry, this is the next page in the B/C/S, page 30. And you're asked: "You said Bosanska Krupa had drafted their own instructions. Is this document you're referring to?" And you answer: "Yes, yes, pursuant to the instructions from the" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Probably the next page for the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, sorry. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you're asked in -- this is line 12 of the English. You said that: "Bosanska Krupa had drafted their own instructions. Is this the document you're referring to?" And you say: "Yes, yes, pursuant to the instructions from the republic [sic] level." Now, in this passage, Mr. Klickovic, you volunteered the information to the investigators that, pursuant to the Variant A and B instructions that apparently meant nothing to you, you in Bosanska Krupa adopted instructions for the work of the SDS party in the municipality; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I repeat that I, as deputy president of the party, the two of us, had prepared instructions long before these. Because Bosanska Krupa was a newly established municipality with 28 local communes and we wanted to unify the activities and the behaviour in all -- in the whole municipality. So we had already worked out something, and when this -- these instructions appeared, we didn't mind, and we referred to them because they were also a product of the laws and regulations on which we based our instructions about the behaviour of the bodies in the Bosanska Krupa municipality. Why didn't I accept this as a valid document? Because everything it contains already existed in the laws and regulations, and I saw this merely as a summary.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry for interrupting you, but you're moving away from my question and repeating something that you've said many times now.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 00242U. And if I could have these two pages added to Exhibit P -- [overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let me come back to his answer. If could you clarify this statement. You said: "Why didn't I accept this as a valid document? Because everything it contains already existed ..." Why does that make a document invalid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The instruction itself as a document has no legal force. Before that instruction, many laws were adopted and many --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. We -- any country has a law that prohibits a theft. If the president prohibits specifically a theft again, that has nothing -- no effect at all? Can the president emphasise what is stated in the law? Just hypothetically.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He can do that. But if that already exists in the laws and regulations we are duty-bound to abide by it. Why reiterate something that's already regulated?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Could these two pages be added to P6662, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add to that P6662, two pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could zoom in on the lower part of this map to -- to show just the map of Bosanska Krupa. That looks perfect. Thank you. Mr. Klickovic, I'd like to ask you now the evacuation order you issued on the 28th of April, 1992, which you refer to at -- in your statement. And if I could get you to first, with the assistance of the usher, trace the line that the Una river -- the path of the Una river through your municipality, Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Una river -- or, rather, Bosanska Krupa is in the Una valley. The Una runs from Drvar where it springs through the Bihac municipality, through Bosanska Krupa, and flows on towards Novi Grad, where it flows into the Sava.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could you please trace the path of the Una through Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if could you circle the eight villages that are listed in your evacuation order and I will recite them to you to remind you. The first one is Ostroznica.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't here. But it must be hereabouts. Veliki Badic and Mali Badic are villages and it's in between there. Mali Badic, Ostroznica, Veliki Badic. Oh, no, I found it. Here it is. This is the town here.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If you could also circle Veliki Badic and Mali Badic.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Zalin.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Veliki Jasenica.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Arapusa.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Veliki Dubovik.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And Potkalinje.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And you agree with what is depicted in this ethnic map that Zalin, Veliki Jasenica, and Potkalinje were in 1991 Serb majority villages?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As local communes, yes. But the populated places themselves, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So they were -- they were mixed. There were Serbs and Muslims [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't understand the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, could you repeat your answer. Interpreters didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at these populated places, Zalin, Veliki Dubovik, Potkalinje, and Veliki Jasenica as parts of their respective local communes, then they had a Serbian majority. But if we look at them as populated places, they were exclusively Bosniak populated.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you agree with what is generally depicted on this map of the municipality that in 1991, almost all of the Serbs lived on the right bank of the Una, on the south side, whereas the left bank, the north side, was largely Muslim; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If you could just initial and date the bottom right-hand corner of this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I would tender that, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will make Exhibit P6663.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Klickovic, when you talk about your order evacuating the Muslim population --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you put your signature, Mr. Klickovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Also today is the 12th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Shall we correct it. Today is 12th. You are ahead of us, Mr. Klickovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, in your statement, at paragraph 13 [Realtime transcript read in error "12"], you discuss your order evacuating the Muslim population from these eight villages you just circled. And you say that you were moving civilians out of the zone of combat operations to the other side of the Una river. Now, when we look at the map, we can see that doesn't make sense as an explanation because these villages are mixed in an area of Serb and Muslim villages, and, in fact, some of these are ethnically mixed areas themselves. So if you were really moving civilians out of the combat zone for their own safety, you would have been moving the Serbs and the Muslims out of this area, not just the Muslim population. In this order, you were just trying to get the Muslims out of an area you claimed for the Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be good if the Prosecution refrained from using terms that cannot be found in the order or elsewhere. "Removal" or "to remove" is a word that cannot be found in these documents. I didn't order for population to be removed but, rather, to be evacuated from the endangered zones. There was also an order about the evacuation of the Serbian population from the other side where they were threatened, and there was also one for the evacuation of -- the evacuation of the Muslim population to the left bank of the Una where they wanted to go and where they would be safer. This was done upon the explicit request of the Muslim representatives with whom we signed protocols about the evacuation, about the time, and place, and method to be applied. In other words, the evacuation was done upon the request of the leadership of those villages, because combat activities had already begun not only along the Una but also elsewhere, and people wanted to be safe. I won't say that anybody was keen on leaving their homes and go elsewhere, but at the time people thought that they would be safer elsewhere and that their safety came above all else. That's why those orders about evacuation, the first, second, third, fourth, were issued. But in keeping with the provisions of Articles 208, 210 of the law, where it says that it -- it's the exclusive authority of the president of the municipality to sign evacuation orders in special circumstances or in war-time conditions.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, you haven't really answered my question, which is: How could this be about removing people from the combat zone for their own safety where you just selectively evacuated Muslims from an area that was mixed Muslim and Serb? That doesn't make any sense, does it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is very clear that the Muslims felt threatened where they were surrounded by Serbs, although they weren't afraid of their neighbours. And I was very clear when I said that everything was done upon the explicit request of the Muslim population who wanted a safer place. Until the war -- the combat operations were over. There was -- there's also a written trace, and there are documents signed by both sides that the population would return when the combat operations were over, and the property would be guarded against those that stayed behind; that is, the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You are aware, are you not, that a couple of weeks after you issued your evacuation order at the 16th Assembly Session on the 12th of May, Dr. Karadzic announced the strategic objectives of the Serbian people, including establishing a border on the Una river, part of goal number 4; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that because I took part in the work and I was an official. But the border on the Una was established long before this. We, even then, didn't wait for that date and for the implementation of strategic goals, but we set up a temporary border on the Una river in agreement with the other side. I am familiar with the objectives, but they did not directly affect the way we worked in the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You are aware, are you not that after Dr. Karadzic announced the strategic objectives at the session, Miroslav Vjestica, the deputy from your municipality, explained that all the Muslims from the right bank of the Una had been evacuated and then said: "Will they have a place to return to? I think it is unlikely after our president told us the happy news that the right bank of the Una is the border."

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I know of this statement by Mr. Vjestica, a delegate from my area, and he was a member of the leadership team together with me. But this doesn't contain the whole text because further on you could see the statement itself and understand its accurate meaning. There had been a problem with the Muslims who were members of the Patriotic League or the Green Berets and it was said of them that there would be no place for them to return to the other side of the Una and that was the official position of the policy of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. And mine too. I was the number one man there. And to my mind, statements can never be the official position of the policy. That can be found in the documents of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa; that is, on the right bank of the Una.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, when you began your cross-examination on this topic, you stated that Mr. Klickovic stated in his paragraph 12 of his statement that in relation to the moving population, or something like that. But I can't find the passage in that paragraph. Was it not included in the redacted one?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, I apologise, Your Honour. I must have misspoke. It's paragraph 13, the second half of the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And a few days after this Assembly session where the strategic objectives were announced, you ordered the evacuation of the remaining population -- Muslim population from the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But you cannot establish a link between that and the strategic objectives of the assembly. We're talking about Zalug and the remainders of a populated place at Bazadzik. People who were my neighbours wanted to go to the left bank of the Una until all that madness, as they put it, was over. It was clearly established. People came to me and asked me if -- for an evacuation to be organised so that they could cross the Una and they felt they would be safe on the left bank among their own police and army, which was the BH army. This was done with the best possible organisation, and those activities were well received because the population that felt threatened remained unharmed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 01061, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is the evacuation order you were just speaking about; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, you said that this was done at the request of the people affected, but this document refers, as reasons for this evacuation, that the political situation is becoming more complex, that Izetbegovic has been threatening members of the Serb army, and, as a result, no personal or collective safety can be guaranteed to the Muslim population if the war escalates. Now, surely, if you had done this at the request of the Muslims affected, you would have put this in your order to make it look less like a criminal expulsion order, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The order is a document which is regulated by regulations. The way it's written is regulated. And an order always contains the subject and a reasoning based on the assessment of the political situation. In this part, which you have just read out, I can't say that Hamdija Arnautovic and Vejsil Palic and the rest of them contacted me and told me why they wanted to go. But it boils down to the following: The situation is getting more complex. Please make sure that we can leave with dignity. They left their houses and the keys to their Serbian neighbours, and when they returned they got them back.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The document says the evacuation should be directed towards Cazin Krajina. That's an area on the left bank of the Una river, outside the territories defined by the strategic objectives; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. The Cazin Krajina is on the left bank of the Una, but 400 square kilometres of the municipality of Bosanska Krupa is in the territory of Cazinska Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And a few days after you issued this order, having essentially eliminated the Muslims from the Serbian municipality, you proposed the cleansing and destruction of property along the left bank of the Una as part of your effort to establish a border on the Una river in accordance with the strategic objectives; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not right. These two things cannot be connected that way. It is very well known why the facilities along the Una river should be neutralised because they're military objectives and they're the target of sniping fire. It is a well-known thing that women and children were killed by that kind of sniper fire, and also from minarets, from mosques, where snipers were. This does not mean elimination. And the destruction of these targets along the Una river does not mean setting a border. It means destroying the sniper nests on the right bank of the Una river that were sowing death.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could we have P2616, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you tendering this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll receive it as Exhibit P6664.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, this is a proposal signed by you, dated the 25th of May, 1992. And under point 1, it refers to carrying out military preparations concerning the cleansing of the left bank of the Una. And under point 2, it says: "In the course of preparations and cleansing of the left bank of the Una, destroy and pull down as many residential and other buildings as possible." And point 3 refers to preparing to blow up bridges across the Una. And the reasons -- the number one reason stated for this proposal is the political determination to have the border of the Serbian municipality AR Banja Luka, Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and Serbian state established along the river Una up to Bosanska Otoka. So contrary to what you said a moment ago, this was part of your effort to establish a thick and permanent border on the Una river; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. You have to view events chronologically. Documents and one's attitude after the strategic objectives is a different thing, those adopted by the Serb Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina and behaviour before that and activities before that are a different matter. This document is entitled: "Proposal." And it is sent to the army. It is sent to the brigade for their consideration and to see -- because the civilian authorities were heavily criticised because of the destruction of housing facilities and on the right bank of the Drina river --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Of the Una river, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that is why we asked for combat to be removed from that area and of course to set up a border, that is to say prepare bridges or destroy them, because the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa did not have forces to defend themselves and to set up a front line since we had 16 territorial dispatches from Cazin Krajina to deal with. And this is a proposal that is sent to the brigade and then the brigade decides whether they're going to do this or not. This is not of a binding nature, and that is why it is called a proposal because otherwise it would have been an order. However, the civilian authorities cannot issue an order to the armed forces, and we knew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, after you had evacuated the Muslims out of the Serb municipality, out of the right bank of the Una river, and established a border on the Una, you stated publicly that the Muslims could not return to the Serb side, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct that they could not return until operations and everything concerning the war came to an end. Before we achieved an agreement with the other side, every three or four days some sabotage groups came and they tried to create chaos by way of these incursions, and that is why we said that at that moment that was justified.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to play a video containing an interview or comments you gave to Banja Luka Television at the time of these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Pardon me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Reporter: What does the representative of the authorities say about all that?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is 65 ter 40639. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Gojko Klickovic: The River Una is the border of the Serbian state of Bosnia-Herzegovina and it is to be expected that the provocations and shooting will continue, because most of the areas where they are located have been ethnically clean areas of the Muslim people even before ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Just pausing there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, that is you talking to TV Banja Luka; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could it be continued -- same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's stop it. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Could it be continued from the -- very second that was stopped?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it it's very short. We'll start from the beginning? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Reporter: What does the representative of the authorities say about all that? "Gojko Klickovic: The River Una is the border of the Serbian state of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it is to be expected that the provocations and shooting will continue, because most of the areas where they are located have been ethnically clean areas of the Muslim people even before, and we have no aspirations to conquer and take those areas, but on the other hand, we will not allow such provocations and we will energetically respond to all provocations, just like we have been doing so far. The situation at the front line, with regard to maintaining the first line of defence, is fairly stable. The morale of the Serbian fighter who are guarding this area and who are guarding the state ... who are guarding the state border of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is very good. When Alija's fundamentalists started this shameful endeavour, they had already been doomed to fail, and the work that we carried out in the first three days is now just being continued; i.e., the borders are being continually reinforced and we can freely say that the border is stable at the moment and arrival of any Muslim formations or Muslim population to this area is not a possibility any longer. They have embarrassed themselves and they have antagonised the Serbian people so much that there is not even a possibility of co-existence and let alone us living together as stated."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm expecting a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The translation has just been concluded. You will hear a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, a moment ago you said that what you had stated at the time was that the Muslims could not return until the combat had concluded but what you actually said at the time on television was that." "... arrival of any Muslim formations or Muslim population to this area is not a possibility any longer. They have embarrassed themselves and they have antagonised the Serbian people so much that there is not a possibility of co-existence and let alone us living together ..."

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And as far as this interview is concerned, I'm really not ashamed of this interview because I said the real truth at that point in time. It is quite clear why I said this at the end. Well, that is because just a day or two before this interview, they had these two sabotage groups that broke in and they killed some civilians in Busevic and a few civilians in a part of town near the sports field although a cease-fire had been signed. And it was stated: Let the Una be there until the stronger ones decide, because we were not the ones down there who decided on war and peace. That is why this statement was made. And we clearly stated that nothing else could be discussed while combat was still going on and while they were still doing what they were doing, while there was sniping from the other side. And you see that we made it clear that we were not interested in the territory where the Muslim population lived and where they lived.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please be asked to speak more slowly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, you are being asked to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, in your answer you say: That is why the statement was made and why we clearly stated that nothing else could be discussed while combat was still going on. But what you said at the time was that the Muslims could not return. Period. Full stop. You didn't say anything about the possibility of them returning after combat ceased; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But I'm not a prophet, and I could not foresee what would happen on the following day or the following ten or 20 days. When statements of this kind are made, one speaks only of the momentary situation and the momentary range of thought in politics that prevails at that point in time. In war-time, everything changes from one day to the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tender this clip, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6665, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Klickovic, in your statement when you talk at length about Dr. Karadzic's character, you say that Dr. Karadzic often cited Njegos to you and others, repeating the line, "A timid chief has no business ruling." Now that is a line from Njegos' most famous work, "The Mountain Wreath," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in essence "The Mountain Wreath" celebrates the extermination by Montenegrins of Muslims -- of Montenegrin Muslims who had converted to Islam, celebrates their mass killing, and the destruction of their homes and mosques, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that's right, and I actually didn't study "The Mountain Wreath" either. The reason why I said this was the following: The president often cautioned us who were working on the ground that we should always give consideration to everything, give it considerable thought, be prepared to make concessions and find a solution that would not hurt anyone regardless of who such a person belonged to. That is why I quoted that, not because of what you are trying to impute to me, because I did not study "Gorski Vijenac."

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 06998, page 84 of the English and page 71 of the B/C/S. And while that is coming up, Mr. Klickovic, you may not have studied "The Mountain Wreath," but it is a very famous poem in the region that you come from, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was born on the Una river, below Mount Grmec, and I'm pretty far away from Montenegro, about 500 or 600 kilometres away. And, I mean, I really never studied literature. I read what I had to read at school. I never studied Njegos or Cosic or anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, perhaps this will remind you of the gist of this poem. This is towards the end where Vojvoda Batric is giving a report to Bishop Danilo on what he refers to as a skirmish with the Turks last evening.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 72 in the B/C/S and this is the middle of the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: He describes this encounter. He says: "As wide and long that Cetinje Plain is, not one witness was able to escape to tell his tale about what happened there. We put under our sharp sabres all those who did not want to be baptised by us. But all those who bowed to the Holy Child and crossed themselves with the sign of Christian cross, we accepted and hailed as our brothers. We set on fire all the Turkish houses, that there might not be a single trace left of our faithless domestic enemy. "From Cetinje we set out for Ceklic. But the Turks of Ceklic all ran away, so we cut down only a few of them, but we also set their houses ablaze. Out of their mosque and of a small building we made a pile of accursed rubble there, as a warning of shame to all people." And then the bishop responds that this news has brought him great gladness and joy. Does that remind you of the fact that this poem celebrates the killing of Muslims, the destruction of their homes, and destruction of their mosques?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for any destruction and any life that is lost during such destruction, I condemn all of that. I think that trying to link President Karadzic to Njegos is unnecessary because Radovan was not a Vojvoda, he was not a bishop either; he was a children's writer, a doctor, a humanist, and these two things really have nothing to do with each other. I believe that this is really being taken out of the context even of good manners, if you will.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm not the one with who linked Dr. Karadzic to Njegos. You did. And now I'd like to look at the line that you specifically state that he repeated often.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 14 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is the very opening of the poem where Bishop Danilo starts by saying: "Lo the devil with seven scarlet cloaks, with two swords and with two crowns of his head, the great-grandchild of the Turk with Qur'an! Behind him hordes of that accursed litter, march to lay waste to the whole planet earth, just as locusts devastate the green fields." Now, here Bishop Danilo is describing Muslims as an accursed litter akin to a plague of locusts; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go into this subject matter. The fact that I used this and provided an answer to the question put by the Defence lawyer on President Karadzic's Defence team, I was explicit and clear. I tried to show how democratic he was in his treatment of people and also I tried to explain what he asked us who were working on the ground to do, those of us who made certain decisions on behalf of the party, and in some situations we had to make do ourselves. So I just mentioned in that context that Radovan often would say to us: Have these tensions eased, easy on the adrenaline, and try to see how you're going to resolve things on the ground without any clashes, without any negative tendencies. That would be all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 16 in the English, page 4 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At the very bottom in the B/C/S, this is Vuk Micunovic responding to the bishop's lament regarding the plague of Muslims in the land. And he says: "Don't, my Bishop, if you have faith in God! What misfortune has come over you now ..." And on the next page in the B/C/S: "... that you do wail like some ... cuckoo-bird and drown yourself in our Serbian troubles? Is today not a festive occasion on which you have gathered Montenegrins to cleanse our land of loathsome infidels?" On the next page in English and about ten lines down in the B/C/S, he says: "Banish, Bishop, such dark and gloomy thoughts! Men bravely bear, wailing is for women. A timid chief has no business ruling! You are not left just to your resources. Do you not see these 500 brave lads?" And roughly 12 lines down, towards the end of his speech, he says: "Beside the youths present here around you, there are six times as many back at home. Their strength, Bishop, is surely your strength too. Before the Turks will have conquered them all, many a wife of the Turk will wear black. Our struggle won't come to an end until we or the Turks are exterminated." Now this is the passage where the line, "a timid chief has no business ruling," appears. And it is clear in context that Vuk Micunovic is using this line to try to encourage the bishop to be brave because they have hundreds of Montenegrins ready to cleanse the land of Turks and they will not stop until they or the Turks are exterminated. In other words, this is part of a call to ethnically cleanse the land of Muslims, is it not?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You've gone far, far away. I just said a single sentence, or to be more precise, a few words that he used, not mentioning this part up and this part down when he wanted to draw our attention to what we should be like; that is to say that we should have a fiery temper, that we should be patient, but that we should work that way, that was his way of operating. Believe me, as for "The Mountainous Wreath," I'm not interested. This is history, way back before me. I don't have time to deal with all of this, let alone something that happened 200 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd tender the pages we referred to in the first page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have no objection, but I just note that I can imagine what your reaction would have been had Dr. Karadzic tried to do something like this. But the door is open, so we don't have any objection, just hope you'll just give the same consideration to Dr. Karadzic on his questions that you have given to Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The witness cited a sentence from this -- is this a poem -- poem? And it's fair enough for the Prosecution to tender this. Shall we admit only those pages referred to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: As far as we're concerned, we can admit the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, you can't understand thing if you don't admit the whole -- whole poem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, the -- the -- emphasise will be on the sentence which reads: "A timid chief has no business ruling." But that -- bearing that in mind, we'll admit those pages shown to the witness. Shall we assign a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6666.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Hmm.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, you said you weren't interested in "The Mountainous Wreath": "This is history, way back before me. I don't have time to deal with all of this, let alone something that happened 200 years ago." In July 1992, at the 17th Assembly Session, Dr. Karadzic said: "Last night at the caucus meeting we talked about Njegos a lot, and we feel that every verse by Njegos reflects the situation that we are now in." That's D92, page 12. Now during the war, did you ever hear Dr. Karadzic compare the events recounted in "The Mountain Wreath" with current events?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have an opportunity to hear that, and I did not attend this session of the assembly and the club meeting in July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In your statement, at paragraph 7, you refer to a visit from Louise Arbour, then the Prosecutor of the ICTY, that took place when you were prime minister. Now that visit was in January 1997; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was that time. That would be right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you say in paragraph 7 that the Prosecutor Arbour inspected some orders issued by Dr. Karadzic and "commented that it was all in order and in accordance with applicable international rules." Now what actually happened at this meeting was that you presented her with 11 documents that had been preselected and provided to her as part of an effort to convince her that the Mladic and Karadzic indictments were unfounded. That's basically what happened, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. The liaison officer for co-operation with The Hague, assistant minister in my government, Goran Neskovic, was given the task of taking all orders that the president signed and to show them. And Mrs. Arbour was also allowed to copy everything and certify everything and take anything she felt was necessary with her. Afterwards, I spoke with my assistant, and he said that the comment was that everything was in order and that she did not see anything incriminating there, in that sense. They spoke as lawyers. It was not 11 orders that were mentioned. I don't know if there were 11 or 10 or 20. All I know is that I said that everything that was available should be made available because there was nothing that we had to hide.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have 65 ter 26006, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Hasn't been released, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Klickovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think we're hearing B/C/S in English channel. It has been sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And I believe the document has been released now, so perhaps we can just call it up.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, this is a report of a Bosnian Serb TV broadcast by the BBC. It's only in English, so I will read the relevant passages to you. It reports on Prosecutor Arbour's visit with you and others, and it says that the meeting took place on the 21st of January and was attended by you; Aleksa Buha; Branko Petric, the justice minister; Dragan Kijac, interior minister; Svetislav Semojevic [phoen], constitutional court chairman; and others. Is that consistent with your recollection about the date of this meeting and who was present?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can say with 90 per cent certainty that the meeting did take place. It was a meeting that preceded subsequent activities of Mrs. Louise Arbour in Pale and an agreement to open an office for the Tribunal investigators in Banja Luka, and these people probably did attend. These were my associates. The ministers -- the date is the 21st of January, so I don't see any reason for it to be different. I think it was that day, that composition, and that topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the report states: "The Serb republic government has taken adequate counter-measures against The Hague Tribunal's bill of indictment against Radovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic." And then it quotes from you stating: "We have prepared 11 extensive documents showing that some evidence cited in the bill of indictment, that is, most of the evidence, does not wash. "We wanted Mrs. Arbour to see the original documents which refute the evidence presented in the bill of indictment, and I hope that this will, to a certain extent, alter their position. Our position on all that they are demanding from us remains the same." Now whether or not it was 11 documents or -- or a slightly different number is besides the point. But what happened at this meeting is that you presented -- your delegation presented the Prosecutor with a number of pre-selected documents in an effort to convince her that the Mladic and Karadzic indictments didn't wash; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But the 11 documents were not orders. She didn't look at those. These 11 documents are something else. If my memory serves me, I think that these were also reports from these foreign teams who were in the field, who recorded the situation, and I think those reports, too, were submitted as evidence that what is -- was cited in the indictment against President Karadzic and Commander Mladic does not stand. That was our professional opinion. And we made it known at the time to Mrs. Arbour that we will continue to work on this, and that the -- we will offer counter-arguments in order to prove that crimes were not on that side but by those who made or formed an illegal state and then began to fight against the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I tendered this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6667, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, you've emphasised both in your statement and in your testimony that Dr. Karadzic's orders were in compliance with applicable laws. Now this Trial Chamber has received evidence that in early February 1998 just after you concluded your term as prime minister, ICTY investigators came to Pale to inspect various archives and in connection with that there is a -- RS authorities took steps to conceal documents they considered incriminatory, and I refer as examples to P3934, P6489, and P6490. Do you know --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say something. Can we have the reference, please. Where does it say that Mr. Klickovic was prime minister still in February 1998? The government changed on the 11th of January, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Perhaps there was a mistranslation. I said immediately after he concluded as prime minister, he confirmed he was prime minister until January 1998.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, do you know anything about those efforts?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because during my time, it did not occur to anyone to conceal any documents, regardless of the nature of the documents. I assert today also, and ultimately I did prove that in my seven-year case, that all the documents of the government, the Presidency, and the president were based on documents that were in force at that time, legal regulations that were enforced at that time. I have nothing to do with anything that happened in 1998. You probably know who came to power in 1998 and which coalition. It was the DRP. And perhaps they did all of these things, but even -- regardless of what that DRP coalition did, they didn't have anything to conceal either.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If they -- if they did. If they did anything. That was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: At paragraph 6 of your statement you describe Dr. Karadzic's intentions as "crystal-clear and honest like those of a child, true and well meant." Would it surprise you, Mr. Klickovic, to hear that Dr. Karadzic was actually directing those efforts to hide incriminatory documents from the ICTY? Would that be inconsistent with the child-like honesty that you perceived in him?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot believe that. Knowing Mr. Karadzic from before as a -- as an author and a doctor, I would never, never accept that he worked to conceal crimes. To write for children, to treat people, and to move around without any security at that time really speaks to the character and the honesty of the man. I often disagreed with the president when I was prime minister, but this calm, cool-blooded approach of his, the tendency to comprise, that was the reason, because, in order to form a state, a country, one has to act more energetically with more force and he simply did not have the required force and strength to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Klickovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Gustafson. Mr. Karadzic, do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we're on the topic of "The Mountain Wreath," I would like to ask Mr. Klickovic to tell us or to confirm - I don't want to be leading - but it's a historical fact, when did Njegos live, and when did he write this poem?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As an intellectual, I will say that as far as I know this was during the Ottoman conquest of the Balkans and the Turkish conquest when there was a lot of burning, looting, destruction, such acts going on in that territory. And at that time Njegos, as a bishop, painting the events that happened in Montenegro at the time or the area of old Herzegovina, because it's not just Montenegro, he put those events on paper in his poem, "Gorski Vijenac," "Mountain Wreath," and others. I'm more familiar with the work of Petar Kocic and Branko Copic from the area where I come from, so I didn't really study Njegos so much. But that is the historical context when Montenegro was constantly attacked from the sea and from land. Every few years those areas would be engulfed in flame and ashes. This is what I can say about the time when that poem was created. We know that Njegos was a spiritual and temporal leader in that period. He embodied both of those personalities. He was somebody to whom the tribal leaders looked up to. These are the historical facts that I am aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we agree, he lived in the first half of the 19th century, and do you happen to know when this alleged incident happened with converted Serbs in Montenegro?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was -- I cannot remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. This will be leading. Is it possible that this was in the 17th century --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, just looking at the historical chronology in that area, it's possible but I'm not sure. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I meant to tell you to move on. Witness didn't remember.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Can we then see from this document, 65 ter 6998, page 091 -- actually, it's the ERN number 091 in the Serbian. That's the last page. 091. To see what Bishop Danilo says here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to find the corresponding English page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 003. Ah, yes, we have it. All right. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you recall how many characters there are in "The Mountain Wreath"? Was it done as -- how many characters are featured there?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the number, but I remember many of them: Vuk Mandusic, Vuk Micunovic, Bishop Danilo, I remember the Iguman. I remember quite a few of the characters. And the main thing is that this epic poem speaks about conquerers and people who come to destroy their land, their homes, their property, their faith. This is the essence. This is what we were taught in history. It was not the Montenegrins who went anywhere. They were on their own land, on their own property, the land of their fathers, and these others came to destroy that, to destroy the people there. And that was the basis for the resistance, for the struggle, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to read from the fifth to the tenth poem?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask for a reference in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Where in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Fifth -- fifth -- fifth line, yeah: "Just as a wolf has the right ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Just as a wolf has the right to his sheep, so has every tyrant to a weakling, to place foot upon tyranny's neck, to lead tyrants to knowledge of the right, this is the most sacred of man's duties." Is this something that is well known among our people? Just as the quote that I said, have these become sayings among the people?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not just this. Even though I didn't study "The Mountain Wreath," there are many verses that just ordinary people use or paraphrase, perhaps they don't know the exact lines of the poem. But Njegos is frequently quoted in all areas, particularly by those who are familiar with the written word. Njegos is considered to be a freedom-loving author, writer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we see what he says about the crucifix and the crescent moon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Where is it? On the same page? With footnote 96, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I think it's on the same page. I'm going to read it in Serbian. I don't know what "crescent" means in English, and I can kindly ask for this to be translated: "Awesome symbols, the crescent and the cross; their kingdoms are the realms of graveyards. Following them down the bloody river, sailing in the small boat of great sorrows, we must honour the one or the other."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What do you think when the bishop says that the crescent and the cross are awesome symbols and that even though we must honour the one or the other, it should be done at the graveyard?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that those two awesome symbols each one of them lead to suffering. Regardless of the fact that the cross is his symbol and the crescent moon, and we know whose symbol that was, he asserts that each of these should be placed where their rightful place should be, and that mostly everything that is happening is, let me put it, epic suffering. In war, of course, people die on each side. Suffering is inevitable. Suffering is something that marks each of the sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to say something else. I don't know what page it is on, but I'm going to ask you if you recognise it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter's note that we are unable to translate "The Mountain Wreath" a vista.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without reference, the interpreters find it impossible to translate.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. I will find the reference after the break, because these are very important lines of the poem because of the Serbian people's understanding of them as their own. They consider them as their own. Now I'm going to go back to the topic of Variant A and B, that paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You asserted here --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. So far then we'll add these page -- this page as well as English page 14 where the -- the dramatis personae appears. So add these two pages to Exhibit P6666. Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry. Maybe I misunderstood, I thought the earlier ruling was to admit the entire document. I don't have a position either way. I just ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think we had -- we need to read all this 100-page poem. I think we admitted only those pages shown to the witness. So we'll add this page, as well as page 14 in English, and together with the corresponding B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that as early as spring - May 1991 - you began preparations for the plebiscite of the Serbian people and preparations for the founding assembly. At that time, did you have any instructions A and B or any instruction from the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In early 1991, in the territories exclusively inhabited by the Serbian people, we organised a debate which we were obliged to do according to the Law on the Referendum. So we organised a debate on the establishment of our own municipality only in areas populated by the Serbian people. So those areas that we mentioned Zalin, Potkalinje, and others, we did not mention them as territorial entities, only the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa. We left them the possibility to join functionally and effectively the municipality of Bosanska Krupa if they chose to do so. There was no paper either from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or any kind of instructions from the central government.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness be shown 65 ter 6738.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Klickovic, I kindly ask you to be as brief as possible in your answers. I will try to keep my questions as brief as possible too. The documents speak for themselves. This is a report on the plebiscite and the referendum of the Serbian people of Bosanska Krupa. And in the second paragraph, it says: "Activities in preparing the Serbian people for the plebiscite and referendum started back in May 1991." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then the reasons are referred to here, why this matter was speeded up, the military data files, the Martic case, and so on and so forth - I would like to tender this document - distribution of weapons and other things. Everything is there in the document. They showed, and this is already on the 2nd of December, 1991, you're saying that the Muslims are getting ready for a settling of accounts with the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had information as to how many weapons there were present on their side in our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4315, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we look at 65 ter 1042, please. I'm sorry. Actually, I will use that document later. 65 ter 17480.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, I don't have time to show the decisions about the study. I'm going to the decision on the establishment of the assembly.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is when the provisional assembly of the Serbian people was constituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And how does this stand in relation to the recommendation of the assembly of the 11th of December or the ANB paper of the 19th of December?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no, that has nothing to do with that. This was done much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of positive laws and the programme of work and agreement with partners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tendered this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm just wondering why we are coming back to these events that has been redacted from his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The Prosecution was trying to imply that these things all happened as a result of Variants A and B and Dr. Karadzic should be entitled to show what happened before.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, just to clarify. I never put to the witness that the Serb municipality assembly was created pursuant to Variant A and B, but the general topic, of course, was covered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we will receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4316, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we take a break? We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I would like to put back the previous document on the screen, only for a couplet. 6998. It's a 065. 65 ter 6998. Has this one been admitted, Excellencies? Sorry, no, we're not done with it. Let's go back so we finish it. I mean, the poetry. 091 in Serbian, 003 in -- this page is admitted. Let's just look at a couplet. Yes, it says here -- actually, the previous page in English. Actually, no, this is it: "Bravery is the lord of all evil, as well as the drink most sweet to the soul."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with this couplet? How is it remembered by the people?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's familiar. The Serbian people often quotes that, in our area too. Figuratively speaking, this is in the souls of the Serbian people in our parts, and we also know what it means.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see page 104 in Serbian. Page 016 in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Human blood is dangerous nourishment." [Interpretation] It says here: "Human blood is dangerous nourishment. It has started gushing out of your nose. You have stuffed your belly with many sins." And eight verses down: "To the cruel men, an empire is no good, except to spread their shame before the world. A savage mind and a poisoned temper as a wild boar, not a human being. He whose law is written by his cudgel leaves behind stench of inhumanity." Are these positions of Bishop Danilo known among our people?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, especially the last two verses. The Serbian people in the area it populates never had a liking for force which is called cudgel here.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add this page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now see one page so we can see how many characters there are. Page 987 [as interpreted] in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, previous page was page 42 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 3987 in English, please. That's the beginning. I don't know the page number in Serbian but we don't really need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please take a look and tell us if these are the characters in this dramatic epic.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the characters. And I remember a good number of them. And I also recognise the others, because I read "The Mountain Wreath." It was mandatory reading at school. And I had the book in my hands a number of times, only I didn't really study it deeply.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think this has been already included. Yes. I said page 14 in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then we are done with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to continue, as briefly as possible, with what you did in the municipality and based on what you did it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would like to have the previous document back on the screens, the one that we saw before this one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, on the 25th of October, you adopted the decision; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you said that you did it long before the --

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We already admitted it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4316, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 65 ter 17479, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is and when it was adopted.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the statute of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, which was drafted for the session of the 11th of December, 1991, when the constituent phase was to be completed. We adopted this document based on the constitution and the Law on Municipalities which precisely lays down how this must be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4317, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 17487, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So, material from the session, it says, of the provision Serbian assembly of Bosanska Krupa, and so on. Let's see the following page -- we see -- we note the date here, 11 December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And it must be temporary until the assembly is constituted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So item 3, sub-item (b), on the agenda reads: "Declaration of the Serbian municipality ..." And item 4 reads: "Adoption of the statute."

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see the penultimate page in the Serbian; that's page 8. It says here that -- actually, I need the previous page in Serbian, although it's repeated here too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In sub-item (a), it reads that you were elected president of the Executive Board with an absolute majority of voices; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And let's go to the last page in Serbian. And the last-but-one in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that you said your thanks but what I'm really interested in, you say that there should be talks with the Bosanska Krupa municipality. Did you declare the whole municipality of Bosanska Krupa the -- the Serbian Assembly? Which is which?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, could you repeat your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is true that the statute that we saw just now, Article 1, paragraph 1, define the territory of the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa. All populated places where exclusively Serbs live are listed there. Although there were enclaves such as Zalin, Potkalinje, and others, we didn't mention those because those were territories where the Bosniak people were living. We did not include them in our territory, not one populated place, not one house that belonged to the Bosniak population at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly - and I'm now looking at the statute - and that's the previous document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll receive this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D4318, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D4317, I'm now looking at Article 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, sir, that on the right bank of the Una, before the war, or if there hadn't been a war, there would have been parts of the Muslim municipality?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what we provided for. It's contained in the statute. And also under the agreement with our friends from Bosanska Krupa, we defined that these populated places should be connected to the -- to their municipality of Bosanska Krupa, not to the Serb municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that point, before the war, or without the war, did we proclaim the Una to be the border of a Serbian republic that was non-existent at the time?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not on anyone's mind. Because Bosanska Krupa had some territories on the left bank of the Una. Ivanska, which is rather a large territory which belonged to the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, although it was on the left bank of the Una.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see P2739. Yes. P2739, this is a Prosecution Exhibit. This is from April 1993. It's a report on the work of the municipal assembly and War Presidency from 1st of January, 1992, till 20 April, 1993. Let's go to the next pages. The last paragraph, let's see if it's here. Maybe it's on the next page. The last two lines in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991, work on the study on the division of the Bosanska Krupa municipality began and so did the establishment of the Serbian municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Let the witness please start over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I have already said that in May, in the local communes populated by Serbia -- by Serbs, we conducted a public discussion about the need of setting up a Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, and we got full support. But we had to make a document, a study about the economic justification of the founding of a municipality. That was a legal requirement, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us see the -- the fifth page in the Serbian. You were asked about the evacuation and the moving out of people. Was that permanent without the possibility of return? How did you phrase it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody moved out. It can clearly be seen in the order that these were mere evacuations. I don't want to repeat what evacuations are because that is also regulated by international law and by our laws and regulations too. And the very word, "evacuation" means to evacuate for the duration of a war or a limited conflict or until some issues are resolved. Evacuation means that after the resolution of the problem because of which the evacuation was done, the population evacuated is supposed to return.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Here, in paragraph 2, the war-time Presidency assessed the situation and adopted the only feasible and appropriate decision at the time regarding the Muslim population that remained in enclaves. And it says that: "The Muslims were offered two solutions" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter cannot see where the accused is reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, interpreters have difficulty locating the passage.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's in the middle of the first paragraph in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says Muslims did not surrender their weapons or they refused to do so totally. And it says that they moved out temporarily. And then the second paragraph on this page, the main reason for adopting the decision on the temporary moving out of the population was the physical safety and security of the Muslim people; is that correct Mr. Klickovic?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, because it was our duty as the War Presidency. Every decision, every order that we passed had to be verified by the assembly once it would convene. And that was one such assembly where we had to show all the documents that we had adopted from the very beginning of the conflict until the 20th of April, 1992. All of these decisions that we adopted as the War Presidency were verified by the assembly through this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it says here "temporary," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That means while the conflict is still on or until the problem is resolved; the problem due to which the evacuation took place in the first place. So the term "evacuation" was used consistently.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 19899, could that please be shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
