utterances.text: While we're waiting, Mr. Klickovic, did you provide accommodation to the Muslims only in the Cazin Krajina or also in your own municipality or elsewhere in Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A number of Muslims from these enclaves were staying at Serb houses, a big family from -- a big family of a colonel of the BH army stayed in my house, and then they were also staying in other villages --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the number -- the names of the village. And could the witness, once again, please be asked to speak slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could start over again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number of Muslims or, rather, their families from these enclaves stayed for a while, for the sake of their own safety, with their neighbours from Arapusa, from Zalin, from Potkalinje. One family and an active lieutenant-colonel of the BH army from that family stayed in my house because this is a neighbouring village next to Arapusa. Others were staying with my neighbours, the Latinovicis [phoen], the Strbac family, the Plavsici [phoen]. We certainly made it possible for these people to find shelter where they would feel safe, until conditions were created for evacuating them safely and securely. The idea was that all people who were supposed to be evacuated should stay within their own municipality, Bosanska Krupa. However, the sniping on the Una river and the use of mortars sometimes made it impossible to cross the Una river, so then people had to go the other way around through Petrovac or through Ripca [phoen] and sometimes through Sanski Most, too. Many stayed in Sanski Most with their friends, with their in-laws. There were a lot of in-laws. So it wasn't strictly stated that somebody had to go here or there or to a particular place. All of this was recorded, though. When each and every family departed, when they would go to where they wished to go, then a written document had to be sent to the War Presidency by the person who was in charge of safely escorting that family to the place where they had asked to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to ask you - but please answer very briefly - Arapusa, in whose territory is that where these refugees from Bosanska Krupa were staying from the 23rd of April until the 1st of May?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arapusa is deep in the territory of the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa. And refugees who left, when -- or, rather, who happened to be there when that part was shelled, they asked, themselves, to leave and to stay in Arapusa because many of them had families there, relatives. They had their own houses. Many of them wanted to be there and that's where they went.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just very briefly now, what does this mean that these first five or six were staying with Veljko Tatarevic? And what is the ethnicity of Veljko Tatarevic?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is a mistake. Tatarevic, well, I know him personally. It's Veso Tatarevic, I think. This is a family from Krupa that went to him because -- because of the International Red Cross and because of our own Red Cross, we asked for records from this family so that we could take flour, detergent, and then also so that if they need medical assistance, that the doctor could go and see them there, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about the religions involved --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could we have a reference to the names again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mira Ogarcina is a Serb. And the other person you mentioned was from a Bosniak/Serb marriage, so they fled because of the operations in Bosanska Krupa from the right bank, and that is where they found their peace and safety, in Arapusa.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to the interpreters. Aleksandro Pelagic and Mira Ogarcina, are they Serbs or Muslims. Those were the names that I referred to and we have received an answer. Could this be admitted please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4319, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now have 65 ter 20237. I'm sorry, it could be P02737. Well, wait. There is a translation too. The 28th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You have a War Presidency in the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, a War Presidency. This was automatic. It's according to the constitution, Article 283. The War Presidency takes over the powers of the Crisis Staff when a crisis escalates and when people resort to arms. All of that is regulated by law, so this is automatic, that a War Presidency becomes active.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell us this now: You issued an order here to evacuate Muslims to Budimlic, Japra, Kamengrad, and Fajtovci. Where are these villages and which entity? I mean at that point in time and which entity where they?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the area of Republika Srpska, the municipality of Sanski Most and part of the municipality of Bosanski Novi, because they had family ties and they had friends there and that's why they wanted to go there. However, in co-operation with the leadership of these municipalities, we made it possible to grant their wishes, to go to Bosanska Krupa, to the left bank, that's what we did. And 80 per cent of them went there, to the left bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were they free to stay in Republika Srpska, in these places where they had been evacuated?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Some of them stayed on until the end of the war, and some of them are there to this day because they got married and, in the meantime, during the war, they built houses for themselves there and became attached to the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know when I made this decision on establishing War Presidencies in municipalities?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the date, but I think that it was later, certainly. I cannot remember the date because it's already a bit ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was the 31st of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the participants, it is P2607. And now could this document please be admitted. And could another one be called up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh yes, yes, yes. P. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, why did you decide this before my decision, and on the basis of what?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, according to the constitution of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1974 and the constitutional amendments from 1976, 1989, and 1990, it was spelled out very precisely what a War Presidency should be. So that is not only a legal obligation, it is also a constitutional category, and I didn't need orders from anyone to do this. Once the conflict broke out in the Una area, I activated the War Presidency because that is the only way in which I could observe regulations of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that still existed at the time and also I am observing the regulations of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina that still existed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. At that time, did you have any contact with the government in Pale?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did. But, really, as for practical solutions, I couldn't get anything from that government because, I mean, well, probably they were operating among these masses of regulations and they couldn't really find their way, so I did not find it necessary to contact them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1042, that would be the 65 ter number that I would like the witness to see now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you explain this to us? We have the English version too. On the 24th of April, there's a War Presidency. And now you're issuing an order here to destroy bridges. Can you tell us why this decision was made and what did you expect on these bridges?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let us clarify this dilemma once and for all. The War Presidency of the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa started operating on the 21st of April, 1992, during a night when an attack took place. It was the police, the reserve force of the Muslim police that attacked Serbs in Arapusa. So that was the moment when the War Presidency was activated. This order is clear because we had received intelligence to the effect that in the area of the Cazin Krajina 16 territorial detachments were equipped and armed, so it was 16:1. That was the ratio. And that required full caution on the part of the War Presidency in order to protect civilians in the territory. That is why we issued this order as the civilian authority there to a military unit, to the commander of the 1st Krajina Brigade, either to protect the bridges or to destroy them, if they cannot protect them. However, it is clearly stated here that the decision is in their hands because we cannot issue a direct order. We can just convey an order to the command but they may or may not carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is this an offensive or a defensive measure from your point of view?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is defensive and protective, and it is in accordance with the laws on defence and protection of one's territory that were in force at the time. Now that we're on the subject, may I add that this was not carried out because the assessment of the military was different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4320, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We saw that you had recommended co-operation talks and negotiations in 1991 and agreements with the Muslim municipality of Bosanska Krupa. Once the war broke out, what was your position regarding contacts and communications? Did you address the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I behaved in a certain way while the joint authorities existed in 1991, and I tried to keep that up, and I wanted to alleviate the situation in order to preserve the population and materiel resources. I had telephone contacts with the president of the Municipal Assembly of Bosanska Krupa, Mehmed Ahic [phoen]. I also contacted other people, Ferid Sertovic. We also tried through telephone contacts and through letters to reach agreement to the effect that without a particular need not to cross from one side to the other, not to have any torchings, and so on and so forth, and I think that I said on the local radio, the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa, I addressed our Muslim neighbours and I had lived amongst them until then. I said that it was pointless for us to resolve problems that have to be resolved by the international community and that we're just pawns there, that somebody is pushing into a conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please be shown 65 ter 18648. We need the first three pages. 18428. 18428.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. This is a document that I sent in written form after appearing at the local radio station to all the presidents of the working Presidencies in the municipalities on the left bank of the Una river. We knew each other personally, we more or less thought the same thing, but we were not able to prevent what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We can see that this is an appeal --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: No, no, this is not the same. No, in -- in English, this is not the same. Maybe it's not translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to take you through this. On the first page, you announce this appeal, and then this is the actual appeal.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The contents. The contents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, here, in the second paragraph, you said that they rejected any peaceful agreement. In the third paragraph, you say that you offered 120 square kilometres of territory to them on the right bank and that they did not want that but that they wanted everything, and they wanted the Serb municipality. And then down there, in the last paragraph, you say: "Allow extremists and ideologists of such ideas to go to the first fighting ranks and let them go to attack Serbs in Serb territories" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not catch the last part of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Let's clarify with the document first. What page?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not the English version. This is not the same document in English. It's not the right document. In the Serbian, it's the appeal to the Muslim people of Bosanska Krupa and the Cazin Krajina. I don't know -- I can see that the first page is translated. I'm not sure about page 2 and 3, however.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The first page was identical with the Exhibit P6664. That was my question. Which was shown during Ms. Gustafson's cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is possible. But this is a collection of 61 pages. The first document without the second and the third page is not clear. The first page is not clear without the second and the third page. Because, on the first page, it says that this is the cover letter for the appeal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I don't think that's correct. The first page is a stand-alone order. I -- I am unable to -- obviously the second page is in B/C/S, but it doesn't -- I see no apparent link between the two. There's no reference on the first page to some kind of explanation. So I think this is something that, if that's Mr. Karadzic's position, [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we show the first page. The B/C/S first page is say it is sometime in June; but the English page say it is May. So -- and -- while B/C/S is of some 60 pages but English has only 11 pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: You're correct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it means we do not have full translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: These are different documents, clearly. You're correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says here clearly: "We are attaching the appeal addressed to the Muslim people of your municipalities," so on and so forth. And then the second and the third page are the actual appeal. Could we look at the third page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here in the first paragraph: "The Serbian people of Podgrmec, never even thought of conquering and attacking the Muslim people on the right bank of the Una and not even mentioning the left bank of the Una, and they did not begin the conflict nor can they be blamed for it either. The Serbian people do not need Otoka Pistajlina [phoen], Jeserski Buzim [phoen], or a single foot of land inhabited by Muslims." And then the end of the third paragraph: "Organise life over there. Don't allow your extremists to make provocations. And you can be sure that the Serbs across the Una will not fire a single bullet?" Was this your position, and how does this activity of yours refer to the -- or relate to the activity of the board of the Serbian Democratic Party?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this was in according with the policy --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... only amazed by the talent of the interpreters. Please put a pause between the question and your answer. Could you start over again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will start from the end. This was the political position and the political principle of the SDS in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was our position, too, in regard to the relations at the local level. We really did believe this. This is what we did, and this is how we behaved. These words that I signed as the president of the War Presidency were also backed by the municipal assembly, by the SDS Municipal Board, by the command structure of the TO brigade at the time, which was part of the armed forces of Yugoslavia. All we wanted was to have no shooting. We didn't want people die in vain. We did not want materiel goods to be destroyed. We wanted the problem to be resolved where it was supposed to be resolved. Because that idea did not come either from the left or the right bank of the Una or the Podgrmecija. We kept to these ideas. That is the real truth. And a month and a half after this appeal, it was very quiet on both banks of the Una river. Everybody went about their regular daily jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please -- we would like to tender these three pages from this document. They can be MFI'd if there is -- while the translation is pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do so.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4321, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked and you also talked about the departures of people. You said that you provided an escort. Can we look at page 13 now from the same document. Sir, this is the 29th of April. Are you able to tell us what was the assignment given to this policeman, Radomir Drobac? Since there is no translation, could you please read all of it, but can you just read slowly.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pass for policeman, Radomir Drobac, individual, Muharem Causevic, Fuad Dzigunovic, and Esad Hasanovic. The above persons are permitted to move to the municipality of Bosanski Novi via Rujiska, Agici in order to provide accommodation for the evacuation of the Muslim population from Arapusa. President." And then this is my signature. I signed the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intention was that every person that was moving in the depth of the territory populated exclusively by the Serbian people and where there were some considerable tensions and problems already at that time, are accompanied by an official from the Serb side who would guarantee their security with their own lives and would not permit any kind of abuse or insults or, God forbid, any kind of attack directed at such persons. Here specifically these three prominent people from Arapusa, Bosanska Krupa, and the third one, Hasanovic, was also from Arapusa, were going by themselves to find accommodation in the Japra river valley in Agici in the direction of the town of Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the territory in the Japra valley was under the control of which forces?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That belonged to the area of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which was later Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, does this constitute persecution and ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, ethnic cleansing and persecution are committed in a different way. It's known how this is done. There is no agreement sought with anybody, no protocols are made, nor are people allowed to look for themselves how they would leave and in which conditions. We all had to provide fuel and transport for evacuation. We will to provide meals for on the way, medical service, escort, doctors, and so on. This is something that does not feature in a -- an expulsion. We saw how this looked when Dudakovic's people came to that territory --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the time-period. And could the accused please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you repeat your question. In particular, the last part.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we tendered this page, 13, from this document, please. It can be MFI'd or added to the previous number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll add this to the -- Exhibit D4321, which was marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please look at page 29 of the same document. This was the 29th of April that we just looked at, and now I would like to look at this document dated the 30th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please introduce the document? Could you tell us what it means.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document drafted as a consequence of the visit of this team and these people that we had in the previous pass -- pass, together with the president of the Assembly of the local community of Donji Agici. They reached an agreement that these 500 persons, estimated number, be temporarily accommodated in this area, which was fairly close to Arapusa from they were -- from where they were supposed to come from. So this is a certificate saying that they went, they reached this agreement down there, and then returned to Arapusa, to our area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the president of the local community, which ethnicity did he belong to? And who was the secretary? Who are the people who confirmed that these 500 persons would be received?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are two persons that I knew personally, Sifet Bajraktarevic and Himzo Alijagic. They were people who were there during that other system and, at this time, who were at the head of the local commune which was inhabited by a majority Muslim or Bosniak population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I tender page 29, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be added and marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were asked who was forbidden from returning to Bosanska Krupa. Were just regular people forbidden from returning so that they would not be persecuted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just ask who were forbidden.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who was forbidden from returning to Bosanska Krupa? Serbian Krupa.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a decision by the Municipal Assembly of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, which lists those who are not permitted to return to the territory of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, or, better said, to the left bank of the Una -- actually, the right bank of the Una. This was all of those people who were found on lists as members of units of the Patriotic League, members of the Green Berets, and members of units, paramilitary units, that were already established at that time in the area of the Cazin Krajina and a number of other places. This was referred to in a decision. I don't know if there were any other categories. I cannot remember that precisely, but this was a decision by the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm afraid that they did not manage to note the names of these groups --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter asks that the names of the groups be repeated, as the speakers were overlapping.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could repeat the names of these groups.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Members of paramilitary groups from the area of Cazin Krajina, who were from our areas. Gazije, Dzamijski Golubovi, Sarganovci, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness 65 ter 6692, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us -- well, you mentioned a decision earlier. Is this the decision that you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that's that decision. I have already said that I don't recall the contents, but I do recall the decision, when it was adopted and what was the reason why the decision was adopted. It also says here members of the Party for Democratic Action, members of paramilitary formations, other enemy -- military members, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4322, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please tell us if there were any Serbs who were not permitted to return during the war?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I think that such a decision of the assembly of the Serbian municipality is in existence. I signed it personally, and the persons are listed there. I think they are termed deserters. They put their families away before the conflict and their property, and they are mentioned in that decision. It exists in my file. And lest I paraphrase it, it might be best to procure it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness please, again, be shown document 18428, page 1. Page 61. 18428. The Serbian variant will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the decision you mean?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is it. And I think that it was adopted at the same session. And the categories are listed here, the categories of persons who are not permitted to return and against whom measures will be taken, if they do, because they committed offences against laws and regulations because they didn't respond to call -- call-ups, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Please read out the first two lines.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "All citizens of Serbian ethnicity who did not respond or return to the call-up of the War Presidency of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa by 1 June 1992, and those who left the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa after that or extended their stay as approved by the authorities, are banned from returning to the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa unless they report to the authorities in charge by 1 October 1992."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You overlapped with the interpretation. Could you repeat.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this be added, attached to the multi-page document that we saw before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Having seen the date of this document, I need to understand the nature of this compilation. Can we see the first page of this document. Mr. Klickovic, could you tell us what this document is about? It's sent to some municipal president of -- of several municipalities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is the cover letter that was sent with the document that I, as president of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, sent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, just a second. Cover -- cover letter of -- which covers next two pages or all of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a letter that accompanies the following two pages that have to do with the appeal. The appeal has two or three more pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the last page of this document. Last page of this document. Page is 61. So this is dated as August. So this is a totally independent document from what we -- from the first page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot tell how the Defence compiled these documents, but that document is independent from this one. This is -- that one is an appeal, and these are decisions taken by the assembly, that were taken during the relevant period.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, if I may explain. This is a collection of documents. They are all independent. The first three pages and the 13th and the 29th and then the 61st. Perhaps we should attribute separate numbers. That might be a better solution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will do so. We'll assign a separate MFI number for page 13 and this page 61.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4323, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, no, no. Page 13 will be assigned as MFI D -- could you repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's MFI D4321.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And page 21.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D4323.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 29, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 29.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And 61, this one?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D4324, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, my last question, hopefully. You said that all decisions that you implemented, as well as what you knew about the central bodies of both the party and the republic were based on the law. You kindly brought a collection of laws and regulations from the area of All People's Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's a collection of all laws and regulations that regulated matters from the level of the republic, down to the level of local communes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us see D8895, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this the title page of that collection of laws and regulations, pertaining to All People's Defence with explanations?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It concludes all instructions, orders, conclusions and everything else that belongs in a collection of laws and regulations meant to be applied in practice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Article 386. Can you tell us what socio-political organisations from top to -- down to grassroots are? This is an article from what law, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an article of the Law on All People's Defence of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina from 1984. It was drafted based on the Law on All People's Defence of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia from 1982, which was the basic legal act.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you now tell us what socio-political communities are? From the top down to grassroots, what socio-political organisations are? What are communities on the one hand, and what are organisations on the other? Or maybe read out this preamble.

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you. The communities are territory and functional units, and depending on the level, federal, republican, municipal, down to local commune level; whereas, socio-political organisations at that time were organisations in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, and there were five: The League of Communists, the socialist front, the youth, the unions and the Subnor. Committees of interest are something of else. They are organised by branches and they are actually based on interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us where the SDS would belong?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The SDS is a socio-political organisation, and in this first phase, I would sooner compare it to the socialist alliance of the working people, which is a -- something like a people's front, although based on its programme it can be qualified as a political organisation. Just like the HDZ and the SDA, they could fall under the League of Communists, as far as its place in the system is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please read out Article 2, paragraph 2 -- actually, I'll read the preamble: "In accordance with this law, own preparations for All People's Defence of the organs of socio-political communities, self-management organisations, and community socio-political organisations and social organisations are: 1, preparations for the manufacture and for services, as well as other preparations for functioning during a war; 2, the organisation, arming, equipping, and training of staffs, units and institutions of Territorial Defence and units and staffs of civil defence." And it continues, but I needn't read it all out. Can I -- can we see the following page, please, up to Article 387. Can you tell us the significance -- what the significance of this law was for the behaviour of the party, the municipality, or the local commune, in war-time conditions?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the basic principle, according to which we had to act at the time. It was binding on everyone, no matter who you belonged to, the Serbian, the Bosniak, or the Croatian people, because this was a law based on a federal law, and it was binding on all entities in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since the Yugoslav People's Army became the defence armed forces under this law in 1982, it loses all offensive or aggressive power, and from then on, it no longer had offensive or aggressive activities as part of its doctrine. In order for the people and all entities to be safe, they were enabled to, in case of danger, organise, prepare, equip, and arm a unit or formation or a group to defend them, even if they were as few as five houses or a neighbourhood. In our case, there was no need for that because the Serbs were members of the armed forces and, hence, they had -- had a right to be -- to arm themselves to -- for defence. The territory -- or, rather, the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa was owned [as interpreted] by the Federal Secretariat of All People's Defence pursuant to its order of the 30th of December, 1992, signed by General Veljko Kadijevic, who was federal secretary. He issued an order to General Kukanjac to arm the territorial brigade of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa under the brigade rule of the Yugoslav People's Army because it -- or, rather, for it to be part of the armed forces of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellencies, I seek to tender Articles 385, 386, 387, 388, 389, 390 and 391, to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I have no objection to them being marked. I'm struggling to see the relevance of this 1982 law, but I'll look at it when it's translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, Mr. Klickovic, was this law in force in 1992?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This law was in force in 1992, not even in 1993 it was annulled either by the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina or -- nor by the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was the only law that was in force at the time when the conflict began, when the war broke out. I think that I even included an order from President Izetbegovic from June, I think, saying that these laws were to govern the activities of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no more questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like this to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you have no objection as to marking for identification those articles that were not discussed with this witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No. Again, I'll look at the document [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D4326. And, Your Honours, just to note, 65 ter 18428, page 13 thereof, will be MFI D4325.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. That concludes your evidence, Mr. Klickovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, you have some --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: With your leave, I would like to spend about three or four minutes on one discrete topic that arose in the re-direct which was in relation to D4319, the list of Muslim refugees accommodated in Arapusa. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have D4319 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic, this was -- this was a document you looked at a few minutes ago, a list of refugees from Bosanska Krupa accommodated in Arapusa between 23 April and 1st of May, 1992. And you explained that these were Muslims accommodated deep in the territory of the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa. Now, Arapusa is one of the villages that you ordered the Muslim population to be evacuated from on the 28th April, 1992, in P2737. So the reason these people were accommodated only until the 1st of May, 1992, is that they were evacuated in accordance with your order of the 28th of April; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you didn't understand my explanation of this list. Asked by the accused, I said that the inhabits of Arapusa, specifically Arapusa, were billeted at Donji Petrovic, Osredak, with their neighbours, because they were afraid of raids and vengeance. When I was shown this specific list, I said that these were refugees or, rather, people who were evacuated during the conflicts through Jasenica to Arapusa, and they found accommodation with relatives, friends, or other citizens at Arapusa, and that is an exclusively Muslim village. And they were put there to receive assistance from the Red Cross and medical protection. I did not say that these people were billeted with Serbian families. We didn't understand each other. These people were -- found accommodation at Arapusa with their friends, acquaintances, relatives, and some of them even had their own houses at Arapusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. But you didn't answer my question which was: These people were then further evacuated out of Arapusa to the left bank in accordance with your order of the 28th of April, 1992; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. Nobody could plan when there would be an all-out attack, a conflict, and when there would be an evacuation. When they were put up in Arapusa, the plan was that they would stay on longer. However, when these problems cropped up, and together with the people from Arapusa, they went to the territory towards the left bank of the Una. Some stayed in Kamengrad, Fajtovci, in these places right on the border of the Serb municipality of Bosanska Krupa. Some went towards Agici, Suvaca, and other places; yet others went straight to the Cazin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And a few months later at the end of October 1992, the village Arapusa was officially renamed Srednji Petrovici - and, for the record, that is recorded in the 21st Assembly Session minutes, P1468 - right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That was a decision passed by the assembly and I insisted on changing that name because that used to be called Srednji Petrovici. So if we go back to our history and tradition, Srednji Petrovici was the name of that village. However, who knows who settled there very early on. Turks, Arabs. The village was re-named Arapusa. And then Serbs who had fled from the left bank of the Una to the right bank fled there and they asked for the name to be changed because the name Arapusa was something that reminded them of Arabs, something similar to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And that's because the root of Arapusa, "Arap," is the word for "Arab"; right?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was in their minds --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Klickovic --

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and what made them ask for this change.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is very simple question: The root of the village name Arapusa is the word "Arap," which means "Arab"; correct?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe yes; maybe no. I don't know. I don't know the origin of this word. It's very hard for me to give a direct answer, and I think that we are here in order to establish the truth. Is this not a quiz show to give yes and no answers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's your language, Mr. Klickovic. Does the word "Arap" mean "Arab" or not?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an ordinary word. It's ordinary vocabulary, but I don't want to say anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Given that it is ordinary vocabulary, perhaps you could tell the Chamber whether the word "Arap" in B/C/S means "Arab"?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] and conversely, the name Petrovic is a common Serb surname. So renaming this village Srednji Petrovici, in other words middle Petrovici, connotes a Serb village, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. Because at the time it was only Serbs who lived there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Just briefly. On the basis of this cross --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: About what? About -- about the renaming?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No. The fate and rights of those -- those ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, just one question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Klickovic, these people who were evacuated, did they have the right to go back to their homes once the right conditions were created? Was that stated explicitly?

utterances.speaker: GOJKO KLICKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is an evident example. We kept records of everything that had stayed behind that the Bosniak Muslims left behind so that once -- once these people got -- came back, they could get everything back or get compensation for their land and livestock, and so on. We handed all of those records to them, too. So once they came back to the area, they would know what they should ask for. So there was maximum protection of persons and property. I am proud of the fact that we did not allow anyone or anything to suffer any adverse consequences, and after all, this is recognition that I have received in that area to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D135 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I said one question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well it's within that question, this question. Just to see how it was regulated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will not allow it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then for the participants, can I just say on page 2 of that document it is written that the command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, do not use your time in that manner. You can raise it in your closing argument. Mr. Klickovic, that concludes your evidence. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson, Mr. Karadzic, the Chamber is seized of your motion asking for an adjournment of two weeks between the conclusion of other evidence and the start of Mr. Karadzic's own testimony. And the Chamber will consider the issue and come back to it as soon as practicable. But before doing so, I would like to know how much time do you envisage for Mr. Karadzic's own testimony?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we had allotted 16 hours to that testimony at the time when we believed it would be given in narrative form and we will be requesting some additional time so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are aware that Chamber's consistent position was not to allow any extension of Defence time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't like to see a situation where the Chamber has to stop Mr. Karadzic's own testimony in the middle of his evidence due to the shortage of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We understand that, but we think that there have been circumstances that have arisen which would warrant an extension of the time that you have given us; for example, having to lead witnesses live like Mr. Stanisic and Mr. Jankovic for things completely out of Dr. Karadzic's control, as well as the changing of the mode of his giving testimony, which, as a self-represented accused we believe he has the right not to be questioned by a lawyer if he didn't want to be. So for all of those circumstances, we were planning on making a motion to ask for additional time so that can he complete his testimony and cover all the allegations of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That will be dealt with when the Chamber is seized of the motion. But speaking for myself, I'm very much concerned about the way in which Mr. Karadzic is spending his time. The previous witness is -- is an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: I -- I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll leave it at that. But before we continue, could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I take it the next witness is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. And his testimony has been ordered to be heard in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll resume in closed session. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.38 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 13th day of February, 2014, at 9.00 a.m. 25
